statement: Holmes resents the holiday: London has taken a holiday from wickedness, and nothing in the street needs explaining.

voices.holmes: London has taken a holiday from wickedness, Watson. I find I resent it.

statement: The afternoon's experiment failed a little after seven, when something on the bench went black and stank.
Holmes's opera glass is French and good; he bought it for the opera and uses it for everything else.

voices.holmes: The eye is the instrument, Watson. The glass merely brings the street nearer.

statement: Holmes has been at the violin on and off since Saturday.
Holmes's monograph upon the ashes of the various tobaccos describes a hundred and forty varieties, with plates.

Holmes knew Watson for a man back from Afghanistan the day they met, seven years ago, come home by way of India and the base hospital at Peshawar. He has never asked where the wound was, and Watson does not say.
The man under the lamp walked in from Hampstead to save the fare: his boots are white to the ankle with the dust of the Heath road, about four miles of it.

voices.holmes: The man under the lamp: his boots are white to the ankle with the dust of the Heath road. That is a fact.

statement: The licensed victualler by the pillar box has kept his daughter out an hour past the time her mother allowed.

voices.holmes: The licensed victualler by the pillar box has kept his daughter out an hour past the time her mother allowed, and will be made to pay for it.

statement: That the boots are dusty is observed; that the man walked is inferred. Nobody else in London notes the difference.

voices.holmes: You will note the difference between those two things, Watson, because nobody else in London does.

statement: Holmes's wager with Watson: if Watson reads both strangers correctly, Holmes will not touch the violin before midnight; if Watson fails, Watson reads Holmes's monograph on a hundred and forty tobacco ashes, plates and all. Holmes holds him to his first answer.

voices.holmes: Read them both and the violin waits until midnight. Fail, and you read my monograph, plates and all.

statement: Watson's reading of the old fellow by the cab rank, given to Holmes as his answer in the wager.
topics: the man by the cab rank
answer: An old soldier, an army veteran: an infantryman, Indian service long ago, lame in the left leg, probably a sergeant.

statement: Watson's reading of the clergyman across the street, given to Holmes as his answer in the wager.
answer: An actor in costume, not a real clergyman: a player learning his lines between performances.

statement: The old fellow by the cab rank, as Watson read him and Holmes conceded: about sixty, an infantryman by his stance, Indian service long ago, an old fracture of the left thigh set in a hurry and healed short, a sergeant long out of the army and still standing like one.

voices.holmes: Infantry; India, and long ago; the left thigh healed short; a sergeant.

statement: The old soldier is waiting for a grandchild: he watches the crowd at the height of a child's head, not a man's.

voices.holmes: I should only have added that he is waiting for a grandchild.

statement: Watson misread the old fellow; Holmes put him right: an old soldier, infantry, India long ago, the left thigh healed short.

voices.holmes: No, Watson. An old soldier: infantry, India long ago, the left thigh healed short.

statement: The clergyman is an actor in costume between the matinée and the evening performance at a West End house, in a melodrama with a clergyman in it: greasepaint at the hairline, new lines in a thin script, and he is not wanted until the second act.

voices.holmes: An actor, Watson, between the matinée and the evening performance at one of the West End houses: a melodrama with a clergyman in it, and he is not wanted until the second act.

statement: Watson read the actor correctly before Holmes said a word. Holmes conceded it.

voices.holmes: You have it exactly, and before I said a word.

statement: Watson read a poor country curate; Holmes put the glass in his hand, and he saw the greasepaint. A point to Holmes.

voices.holmes: You saw a black coat and stopped looking.

statement: We see what asks to be seen. A man who asks nothing of anybody might pass under the window every evening for a year and never once be looked at.

voices.holmes: We see what asks to be seen.
